title: MERICS China Essentials Special Issue: EU-China economic relations enter a critical phase
gist: After EU leaders hardened trade defenses in mid-October, MERICS assesses how Beijing might retaliate (non-essential exports first, rare-earth licensing as the key lever) and argues the hybrid-vehicle deal, only 2.06% of Chinese exports to the EU, is symbolic and merely postpones confrontation.

themes.theme: Beijing's retaliation playbook against EU derisking

insights.claim: If the EU hardens trade defenses, China is likely to retaliate first against high-volume European exports it has little strategic need for, such as French cognac, Swedish salmon, fashion, cosmetics and luxury cars.
insights.speaker: MERICS
insights.so_what: European consumer, luxury and agri-food exporters carry the first-line retaliation risk.

insights.claim: Chinese restrictions on foreign financial services providers or on advanced European machinery and components are possible but likely only a last resort, because they would deprive China of international finance and of goods it still depends on.
insights.speaker: MERICS
insights.so_what: Escalation to capital goods or finance would signal a genuine break rather than signaling.

insights.claim: Rare earths offer Beijing maximum impact on Europe with negligible effect on Chinese exports, and rare-earth refining and battery-manufacturing equipment are also useful levers to derail European derisking.
insights.speaker: MERICS
insights.so_what: Rare-earth export licensing is the most credible escalation channel; watch European magnets and battery supply chains.
insights.locator: Beijing could also tighten export restrictions

insights.claim: Beijing will likely keep exempting critical inputs that China itself needs, such as German machine tools, French metrology instruments and Dutch lithography machines, as it did for key US goods in the 2025 US-China trade war.
insights.speaker: MERICS
insights.so_what: Chinese restrictions are likely to be selective, so broad-based supply cutoffs are less probable than targeted ones.
insights.locator: Beijing could also tighten export restrictions

insights.claim: For now Beijing is unlikely to block high-value exports like EV batteries or car parts to Europe, because it is counting on exports for growth.
insights.speaker: MERICS
insights.so_what: Supports a base case of continued Chinese EV and battery exports into the EU despite tensions.
insights.locator: Beijing could also tighten export restrictions

insights.claim: MERICS argues Europe must show it has the stomach for economic conflict and prepare to restrict China's access to European technologies and markets at short notice to create a credible deterrent.
insights.speaker: MERICS
insights.so_what: Points to possible EU counter-measures on technology and market access, a policy-risk factor for companies exposed to China.
insights.quote: It must prepare to restrict China’s access to European technologies and markets at short notice

themes.theme: Hybrid vehicle deal is symbolic, not a breakthrough

insights.claim: Hybrid vehicles were only 2.06% of Chinese exports to the EU in January-August 2026, up from 0.95% in 2025, so the October moderation deal on hybrid exports has limited economic impact.
insights.speaker: MERICS
insights.so_what: The deal gives European carmakers little relief against Chinese imports and does not change the trade balance.

insights.claim: Ursula von der Leyen acknowledged that progress in one sector cannot fix China's huge trade surplus with the EU, signaling the hybrid deal, which included pledges of better market access and reliable rare-earth supply, was more symbolic than practical.
insights.speaker: MERICS
insights.so_what: Expect continued EU trade-defense escalation rather than de-escalation.

insights.claim: Berlin, Paris and Brussels frame the EU-China trade conflict as structural and unresolved despite the October 9 shared understanding on hybrid vehicles, and call the deficit with China structural and unsustainable.
insights.speaker: MERICS
insights.so_what: EU policy direction is toward tougher measures; trade-exposed sectors should price continued friction.

insights.claim: Chancellor Merz said Germany and Europe will no longer stand idly by while other countries harm their economy through subsidies, devalued currencies, overcapacity and aggressive pricing, and is courting Singapore, South Korea and Japan to reduce one-sided dependencies.
insights.speaker: MERICS
insights.so_what: Germany is diversifying trade partnerships in Asia, which may shape supply-chain reallocation.

insights.claim: The EU has new tools available or in preparation: the DiversifyEU initiative to accelerate derisking, a Solidarity Mechanism to counter coercion or retaliation, and a new instrument to limit access to the single market.
insights.speaker: MERICS
insights.so_what: These instruments are the channels through which new restrictions on Chinese goods could arrive.

insights.claim: Emmanuel Macron called for the EU to consider new measures targeting chemicals, plastics and ferro-alloys, pointing to potential new trade flashpoints.
insights.speaker: MERICS
insights.so_what: Chemicals, plastics and ferro-alloys producers face possible new EU trade measures or Chinese retaliation.

insights.claim: MERICS analyst Aurelio Insisa judges the hybrid deal likely only postpones a confrontation that Beijing feels confident of winning, and a full-blown escalation cannot be ruled out.
insights.speaker: MERICS
insights.so_what: Treat the carmaker relief as temporary; tail risk of EU-China escalation remains.
insights.quote: only postpone a confrontation that Beijing feels confident of winning

insights.claim: Chinese state media portrayed EU trade barriers as a protectionist fix for Europe's home-grown problems, insisting China is not the cause of Europe's woes and that a trade conflict would hurt both sides given intertwined supply chains.
insights.speaker: MERICS
insights.so_what: Beijing's public narrative offers little room for concessions on the structural trade imbalance.

insights.claim: A Chinese commentary warned that sincerity is not one-sided and patience is not without limits, signaling irritation at France and Germany's push to reduce supply dependencies.
insights.speaker: MERICS
insights.so_what: Rhetorical warning that Chinese patience in talks is conditional.
insights.quote: sincerity is not one-sided, and patience is not without limits

insights.claim: The tone of Chinese commentary reflects growing confidence in China's development model and economic strength, even though new EU trade instruments could still bring Beijing to the negotiating table.
insights.speaker: MERICS
insights.so_what: Beijing is less likely to yield without credible EU leverage, so EU instruments matter for negotiation outcomes.

insights.claim: Under the early-October deal the EU committed to resolving priority dual-use export licensing cases to China in return for Beijing continuing to expedite critical-mineral export decisions, effectively treating two very different systems as equivalent bargaining chips.
insights.speaker: MERICS
insights.so_what: The deal strengthens Beijing's ability to use rare-earth licensing as a political weapon.
insights.locator: Europe retains fast track for rare-earth licenses

insights.claim: The latest deal does not guarantee rare-earth shipments to European companies; China's promise to speed up licensing last year has produced slow and uneven progress.
insights.speaker: MERICS
insights.so_what: European magnet-dependent manufacturers remain exposed to licensing delays despite the deal.
insights.locator: Europe retains fast track for rare-earth licenses

insights.claim: Despite EU mining, processing and recycling projects announced over the last 18 months, none has yet delivered alternative rare-earth supply, and Europe has not cut dependence on Chinese supplies even though China began licensing critical minerals in 2023.
insights.speaker: MERICS
insights.so_what: Non-Chinese rare-earth supply for Europe is still a long way off, supporting the case for ex-China supply-chain projects.
insights.locator: Europe retains fast track for rare-earth licenses

insights.claim: China retaliated politically through export controls in July by banning dual-use shipments to 14 European companies a day after the EU sanctioned 14 Chinese companies over alleged support for Russia's war in Ukraine.
insights.speaker: MERICS
insights.so_what: Shows China will respond quickly and symmetrically with export controls, a reference for modeling future retaliation.
insights.locator: Europe retains fast track for rare-earth licenses

insights.claim: Beijing benefits from keeping the 2025 licensing rules in place as a bargaining chip, keeping a hand on the switch while Europe struggles to derisk.
insights.speaker: MERICS
insights.so_what: Expect licensing to stay discretionary; rare-earth supply risk is a persistent premium for European industry.
insights.quote: keeping a hand on the switch while Europe struggles to derisk

themes.theme: China Digest: macro, tech controls and policy items

insights.claim: China's economy grew 4.5% in the third quarter, in line with the 4.5%-5% full-year target, driven largely by exports and prompting trade partners' complaints about imbalances and unfair competition.
insights.speaker: MERICS
insights.so_what: Export-led growth sustains the imbalance that fuels Western trade-defense measures.

insights.claim: The People's Bank of China granted Visa approval to operate a card business in China, though the market is now dominated by QR code payments.
insights.speaker: MERICS
insights.so_what: A positive signal on openness but commercial upside for Visa is limited by QR payment dominance.

insights.claim: One-third of Beijing's residents are expected to be aged 60 or above by 2035, and policymakers are discussing raising pensions to stimulate domestic consumption.
insights.speaker: MERICS
insights.so_what: Ageing-driven pension and consumption policy could be a domestic-demand lever.

insights.claim: The US Department of Homeland Security ordered federal civilian agencies to remove DeepSeek products and restrict procurement, including third-party products incorporating DeepSeek technology.
insights.speaker: MERICS
insights.so_what: Restrictions on Chinese AI extend to downstream applications, raising compliance risk for products embedding DeepSeek.

insights.claim: China proposed adding 40 technologies to its prohibited and restricted export catalogue, including 23 AI technologies, with public consultation closing November 15.
insights.speaker: MERICS
insights.so_what: Tighter Chinese AI export control would limit cross-border AI technology flows; watch the final list after November 15.

insights.claim: China revised its drone export controls, with simplified registration for some civilian exports but continued controls on dual-use technologies, effective 18 November.
insights.speaker: MERICS
insights.so_what: Drone makers and component suppliers face changed export compliance from 18 November.

insights.claim: The New Yalu River Bridge between China and North Korea, built in 2014, officially opened on 15 October after a 12-year delay.
insights.speaker: MERICS
insights.so_what: Marginal increase in China-North Korea economic connectivity.
